name: Proposition
quick: A statement that is either true or false.
definition: A proposition makes a definite claim. Knowing whether the claim is true is not required for it to be a proposition. A question or command does not assert a truth value, and a sentence with an unspecified input may need that input supplied first.
example: “Seven is less than three” is a false proposition. “Is it raining?” is a question, not a proposition.
confusion: False statements can be propositions; proposition does not mean true statement.

name: Truth value
quick: Whether a proposition is true or false.
definition: Classical propositional logic uses two truth values, usually abbreviated T and F. A compound statement’s truth value is determined by its components and the logical operators joining them.
example: When p is true and q is false, p AND q is false because AND requires both components to be true.
confusion: A truth value describes a claim, not how confidently someone believes it.

name: Logical operator
quick: A rule for forming a statement from one or more statements.
definition: Logical operators specify how the truth of a compound statement depends on its inputs. Negation takes one input. Conjunction, disjunction, implication, and biconditional take two inputs in their simplest forms.
example: NOT reverses a truth value. AND is true only if both inputs are true.
confusion: An operator’s formal meaning may be more precise than the corresponding word in everyday conversation.

name: Truth table
quick: A table listing every possible input assignment and the resulting truth values.
definition: Each row gives one choice of true or false for every independent propositional variable. Additional columns evaluate intermediate expressions. With n independent variables, there are 2 to the power n input rows because each variable has two choices.
example: For p and q, use TT, TF, FT, and FF. Two formulas are equivalent if their output columns agree in all four rows.
confusion: Checking a few selected rows cannot establish equivalence if other possible rows remain unchecked.

name: Negation
quick: The statement that the original proposition is not true.
definition: Negation reverses the truth value: NOT p is false when p is true and true when p is false. A correct verbal negation must cover exactly the cases excluded by the original, including boundary cases.
example: The negation of “the temperature is above 20” is “the temperature is at most 20,” including exactly 20.
confusion: A phrase that sounds opposite can fail to cover all remaining cases.

name: Conjunction
quick: An AND statement, true exactly when both components are true.
definition: Conjunction imposes both requirements at once. Either false component makes the whole conjunction false. Repeating or reordering the same requirements does not change which truth assignments satisfy them.
example: Having a ticket AND identification requires both items. Neither item alone is enough.
confusion: AND does not mean that one event causes another or happens before it.

name: Disjunction
quick: An inclusive OR statement, true when at least one component is true.
definition: Mathematical OR includes the case in which both components are true. The only false case is when both are false. This inclusive meaning is the default unless an exclusive condition is stated.
example: “Teaching or research experience” allows teaching, research, or both.
confusion: Do not silently interpret OR as “one but not both.”

name: Exclusive OR
quick: An OR statement that is true when exactly one input is true.
definition: Exclusive OR, abbreviated XOR, differs from inclusive OR in the both-true case. Exactly one input must be true and the other false.
example: “Soup or salad, but not both” expresses exclusive OR when those are the two choices.
confusion: The ordinary logical OR symbol does not include this exclusivity by itself.

name: Implication
quick: An IF–THEN statement, false only when its condition is true and its promised result is false.
definition: An implication says that whenever its antecedent holds, its consequent holds. If the antecedent is false, that promise has not been violated. This truth rule does not claim that the antecedent causes the consequent.
example: “If an integer is divisible by four, it is even” forbids a number divisible by four that is not even.
confusion: Knowing the promised result holds does not establish that this particular condition held.

name: Antecedent
quick: The condition after IF in an implication.
definition: In “if p, then q,” p is the antecedent. The implication makes its promise about cases where p is true. The condition may itself be a compound formula.
example: In “if the door is locked, a key is needed,” the antecedent is “the door is locked.”
confusion: The antecedent is not necessarily true merely because an implication containing it is true.

name: Consequent
quick: The promised result after THEN in an implication.
definition: In “if p, then q,” q is the consequent. The implication requires q in every case where p holds, but q may hold for other reasons too.
example: If rain makes a pavement wet, wetness is the consequent. A sprinkler might also make it wet.
confusion: Affirming the consequent does not justify concluding the antecedent.

name: Truth assignment
quick: A choice of a truth value for each propositional variable.
definition: A propositional variable, such as p or q, stands for a proposition. An assignment selects true or false for each such variable. Evaluating a formula under that assignment means applying its operators to those selected inputs.
example: Choose p = T and q = F. Then p OR q is true while p AND q is false.
confusion: An assignment is one row of possibilities, not a proof that a formula is always true.

name: Converse
quick: The implication obtained by exchanging the condition and result.
definition: The converse of “if p, then q” is “if q, then p.” It reverses the direction without negating either part. Its truth need not match that of the original statement.
example: The converse of “divisible by four implies even” is “even implies divisible by four,” which fails at six.
confusion: Reversing an implication is not an equivalence rule.

name: Inverse of an implication
quick: The implication obtained by negating both parts without exchanging them.
definition: The inverse of “if p, then q” is “if not p, then not q.” It is equivalent to the converse, but neither is generally equivalent to the original.
example: “If an integer is not divisible by four, it is not even” is false at six.
confusion: This use of inverse is different from an inverse function.

name: Contrapositive
quick: The implication obtained by exchanging and negating both parts.
definition: The contrapositive of “if p, then q” is “if not q, then not p.” Both statements rule out the same bad case: p true and q false. They are therefore logically equivalent.
example: “If divisible by four, then even” has contrapositive “if not even, then not divisible by four.”
confusion: Both reversing and negating are required; doing only one gives another statement.

name: Logical equivalence
quick: Having the same truth value for every possible assignment.
definition: Equivalent formulas can replace one another inside a larger formula without changing its truth conditions. Equivalence is stronger than agreeing on one particular assignment. A complete truth table can establish it by matching all rows.
example: NOT NOT p and p agree whether p is true or false. In contrast, p and q agree on some assignments but disagree on others.
confusion: Do not confuse a true biconditional on one assignment with equivalence across all assignments.

name: Counterexample
quick: One allowed case that violates a general claim.
definition: A statement about every applicable case is false if even one applicable case fails. For an implication, a counterexample must satisfy the condition and violate the promised result. To disprove equivalence, find an assignment where the two formulas differ.
example: Six is a counterexample to “every even integer is divisible by four.”
confusion: A case outside the claim’s conditions cannot disprove it.

name: Necessary condition
quick: A requirement that must hold whenever the stated outcome holds.
definition: If p implies q, then q is necessary for p: p cannot hold without q. A necessary condition may still be insufficient by itself. The phrase “p only if q” expresses this same direction.
example: Being even is necessary for being divisible by four, but six shows that being even alone is insufficient.
confusion: Necessary describes what cannot be missing, not what guarantees the outcome by itself.

name: Sufficient condition
quick: A condition that guarantees the stated outcome.
definition: If p implies q, then p is sufficient for q. Whenever p is true, q must follow. There may be other ways for q to hold, so p need not be necessary.
example: Being divisible by four is sufficient for being even, but it is not the only way to be even.
confusion: The words sufficient and necessary describe opposite sides of the same implication.

name: Biconditional
quick: An IF AND ONLY IF statement asserting both implication directions.
definition: The statement p if and only if q is true when p and q have matching truth values. It combines “p implies q” with “q implies p.” The abbreviation iff has exactly this meaning.
example: For integers, “n is even iff n is divisible by two” asserts both descriptions apply together.
confusion: An implication in only one direction does not establish a biconditional.

name: De Morgan’s laws
quick: Rules for negating AND or OR by negating both parts and swapping the connective.
definition: Not both p and q means at least one of them is false. Neither p nor q means both are false. These two observations give the corresponding logical equivalences and later have parallel forms for sets.
example: “It is not true that both doors are locked” means at least one door is unlocked; it does not require both to be unlocked.
confusion: Negating each part without swapping AND and OR changes the claim.

name: Double negation
quick: Negating twice returns the original truth value.
definition: The first NOT reverses true and false, and the second reverses them back. This permits replacing NOT NOT p with p in classical logic.
example: If p is false, NOT p is true and NOT NOT p is false again.
confusion: Two negations cancel; a single negation does not.

name: Idempotent law
quick: Repeating the same input to AND or OR leaves it unchanged.
definition: Both p AND p and p OR p have the same truth value as p. The extra copy adds neither a new requirement nor a new alternative.
example: “Bring a ticket and bring a ticket” still requires a ticket.
confusion: This is not a license to delete a different input.

name: Commutative law
quick: Exchanging the inputs of AND or OR leaves the result unchanged.
definition: AND requires both inputs and OR requires at least one. Neither depends on the order of those inputs. Implication does depend on their order.
example: p AND q is equivalent to q AND p.
confusion: An implication cannot be reversed just because AND and OR commute.

name: Associative law
quick: Regrouping repeated ANDs or repeated ORs leaves the result unchanged.
definition: When all three inputs use the same connective, parentheses may move. Three AND requirements must all hold; three OR alternatives require at least one to hold.
example: (p OR q) OR r and p OR (q OR r) admit the same assignments.
confusion: Mixed AND and OR expressions cannot be regrouped by this law alone.

name: Distributive law
quick: A rule for expanding an AND across OR, or an OR across AND.
definition: A shared AND requirement applies to each OR alternative. Conversely, an OR alternative can satisfy each of two AND requirements. In propositional logic both distributive forms hold.
example: A ticket AND either passport OR licence means ticket-and-passport OR ticket-and-licence.
confusion: Keep the shared part in both expanded groups.

name: Logical factoring
quick: Using a distributive law backward to expose a shared part.
definition: Factoring joins repeated requirements or alternatives into one shared expression. It is useful when the remaining terms simplify, for example to “q or not q.”
example: (p AND q) OR (p AND NOT q) factors to p AND (q OR NOT q), which simplifies to p.
confusion: Factoring is an equivalence transformation, not an instruction to choose one case and discard another.

name: Absorption law
quick: Removing a nested requirement or alternative already settled by the outer one.
definition: If p is already an OR alternative, p AND q adds no new successful case. If p is already required by AND, p OR q imposes no additional demand.
example: p OR (p AND q) has exactly the same truth values as p.
confusion: Absorption requires the repeated part in the correct positions; arbitrary terms cannot be dropped.

name: Identity law
quick: Combining with an inactive truth value leaves the other input unchanged.
definition: AND with T adds no extra requirement, and OR with F adds no successful alternative. These are the two identity laws for logical AND and OR.
example: p AND T is equivalent to p; p OR F is also equivalent to p.
confusion: OR with T and AND with F are domination laws instead.

name: Domination law
quick: One decisive truth value settles the entire AND or OR.
definition: An OR with a true input is already true. An AND with a false input is already false. No value of the other input can change those outcomes.
example: p OR T is T, while p AND F is F.
confusion: Do not confuse domination with an identity law, which leaves p rather than a constant.

name: Tautology
quick: A formula true under every possible truth assignment.
definition: A tautology has no false row in its truth table. It expresses a truth pattern independent of the particular input values. It is therefore satisfiable, but satisfiability alone is weaker.
example: p OR NOT p is always true because one of those two alternatives must hold.
confusion: One true assignment does not establish a tautology.

name: Contradiction
quick: A formula false under every possible truth assignment.
definition: A contradiction has no true row in its truth table. No assignment satisfies it. In a proof, deriving such an impossibility can show that a proposed assumption cannot hold.
example: p AND NOT p is always false: the two requirements cannot hold together.
confusion: A formula false in one particular case need not be a contradiction.

name: Contingent formula
quick: A formula true on some assignments and false on others.
definition: A contingent formula is neither a tautology nor a contradiction. Its truth genuinely depends on which values its inputs receive.
example: p AND q is true on TT and false on the other three assignments.
confusion: Contingent does not mean vague or undecidable; it describes variation across assignments.

name: Argument
quick: Premises together with a conclusion claimed to follow from them.
definition: Premises are the statements offered as starting assumptions. The conclusion is the statement the reasoning aims to establish from them. Logical validity asks whether those premises can all be true while the conclusion is false.
example: “If rain, then wet pavement; rain; therefore wet pavement” has two premises and one conclusion.
confusion: An argument is a structure of reasoning, not necessarily a dispute.

name: Validity
quick: The impossibility of true premises together with a false conclusion.
definition: An argument is valid when every assignment satisfying all its premises also satisfies its conclusion. This concerns logical form. Whether its premises are actually true is a separate question.
example: Modus ponens is valid because p true and p implies q true force q true.
confusion: A true conclusion alone does not make the reasoning used to reach it valid.

name: Inference rule
quick: A reusable valid pattern for moving from premises to a conclusion.
definition: An inference rule specifies the premises that justify a conclusion. To apply it, identify a precise match between the actual statements and the pattern. A formula can replace a single letter in a pattern, but repeated letters must mean the same formula.
example: From p and p implies q, modus ponens permits q.
confusion: Do not use a rule if one of its required premises is missing.

name: Modus ponens
quick: From p and “if p, then q,” conclude q.
definition: This pattern affirms the condition of an implication. The implication gives a promise, and the other premise establishes that its condition holds. Together they force the promised result.
example: If a file is saved then a copy exists; the file is saved; therefore a copy exists.
confusion: Knowing q instead of p does not fit this rule.

name: Modus tollens
quick: From “if p, then q” and NOT q, conclude NOT p.
definition: If the antecedent held, the consequent would have to hold. Denying that consequent therefore rules out the antecedent. This is the contrapositive reasoning pattern.
example: If divisible by four then even; not even; therefore not divisible by four.
confusion: The negative premise must deny the consequent, not the antecedent.

name: Hypothetical syllogism
quick: Chain “p implies q” and “q implies r” to obtain “p implies r.”
definition: The shared middle condition connects two conditional promises. If p were true, the first premise would give q and the second would then give r. The conclusion remains conditional.
example: Accepted applications are reviewed; reviewed applications receive responses; therefore accepted applications receive responses.
confusion: The argument does not establish that any application was actually accepted.

name: Disjunctive syllogism
quick: From p OR q and NOT p, conclude q.
definition: At least one of the two alternatives must hold. Ruling one out leaves the other. Inclusive OR is sufficient because the negative premise excludes the both-true case as well.
example: The key is in the drawer or pocket; it is not in the drawer; therefore it is in the pocket.
confusion: The OR premise must actually cover the possibilities claimed; an overlooked third location undermines that premise.

name: Affirming the consequent
quick: The invalid pattern of inferring p from “p implies q” and q.
definition: The consequent might hold for another reason. An assignment with p false and q true keeps both premises true but makes the proposed conclusion false.
example: Rain implies wet pavement; the pavement is wet; therefore rain. A sprinkler gives a counterexample.
confusion: This is different from modus ponens, which also establishes p as a premise.

name: Denying the antecedent
quick: The invalid pattern of inferring NOT q from “p implies q” and NOT p.
definition: An implication does not say that its antecedent is the only way the consequent can hold. With p false and q true, both premises are true and the proposed conclusion is false.
example: No rain does not imply dry pavement: a sprinkler may have wet it.
confusion: This is different from modus tollens, whose negative premise is NOT q.

name: Satisfiability
quick: Having at least one truth assignment that makes a formula true.
definition: A satisfying assignment is a choice of input truth values on which the formula is true; it is also called a model in propositional logic. Unsatisfiable means there is no such assignment. SAT is the problem of deciding whether one exists.
example: p AND q is satisfied by p = T, q = T. p AND NOT p is unsatisfiable.
confusion: Satisfiable means at least one successful assignment, not every assignment.

name: ¬ — Negation
quick: The statement that the original proposition is not true.
definition: Negation reverses the truth value: NOT p is false when p is true and true when p is false. A correct verbal negation must cover exactly the cases excluded by the original, including boundary cases.
example: The negation of “the temperature is above 20” is “the temperature is at most 20,” including exactly 20.
confusion: A phrase that sounds opposite can fail to cover all remaining cases.

name: ∧ — Conjunction
quick: An AND statement, true exactly when both components are true.
definition: Conjunction imposes both requirements at once. Either false component makes the whole conjunction false. Repeating or reordering the same requirements does not change which truth assignments satisfy them.
example: Having a ticket AND identification requires both items. Neither item alone is enough.
confusion: AND does not mean that one event causes another or happens before it.

name: ∨ — Disjunction
quick: An inclusive OR statement, true when at least one component is true.
definition: Mathematical OR includes the case in which both components are true. The only false case is when both are false. This inclusive meaning is the default unless an exclusive condition is stated.
example: “Teaching or research experience” allows teaching, research, or both.
confusion: Do not silently interpret OR as “one but not both.”

name: → — Implication
quick: An IF–THEN statement, false only when its condition is true and its promised result is false.
definition: An implication says that whenever its antecedent holds, its consequent holds. If the antecedent is false, that promise has not been violated. This truth rule does not claim that the antecedent causes the consequent.
example: “If an integer is divisible by four, it is even” forbids a number divisible by four that is not even.
confusion: Knowing the promised result holds does not establish that this particular condition held.

name: ↔ — Biconditional
quick: An IF AND ONLY IF statement asserting both implication directions.
definition: The statement p if and only if q is true when p and q have matching truth values. It combines “p implies q” with “q implies p.” The abbreviation iff has exactly this meaning.
example: For integers, “n is even iff n is divisible by two” asserts both descriptions apply together.
confusion: An implication in only one direction does not establish a biconditional.

name: ≡ — Logical equivalence
quick: Having the same truth value for every possible assignment.
definition: Equivalent formulas can replace one another inside a larger formula without changing its truth conditions. Equivalence is stronger than agreeing on one particular assignment. A complete truth table can establish it by matching all rows.
example: NOT NOT p and p agree whether p is true or false. In contrast, p and q agree on some assignments but disagree on others.
confusion: Do not confuse a true biconditional on one assignment with equivalence across all assignments.

name: ∴ — Therefore
quick: Introduces the conclusion drawn from the preceding premises.
definition: The therefore symbol marks the move from the stated premises to the proposed conclusion. Whether that conclusion is justified depends on the argument; the symbol itself does not prove validity.
example: p, p → q ∴ q reads: p, and if p then q; therefore q.
confusion: Writing therefore before a statement does not establish that it follows from the premises.

name: ⊢ — Derivable from
quick: The conclusion on the right can be derived from the premises on the left.
definition: The turnstile separates starting premises from a conclusion obtainable by the stated proof rules. It describes a derivation rather than a numerical comparison. The letters P₁ through Pₙ stand for the individual premises, and C stands for the conclusion.
example: p, p → q ⊢ q records the modus ponens derivation of q from those two premises.
confusion: The turnstile is not the divisibility symbol or a logical AND.

name: Conjunct
quick: One of the parts joined by AND.
definition: The whole AND expression is a conjunction, while its individual joined parts are conjuncts. A conjunct may itself be a compound formula. Every conjunct must be true for the conjunction to hold.
example: In p AND (q OR r), the conjuncts are p and the whole expression q OR r.
confusion: Conjunct names a component, not the entire conjunction.

name: Disjunct
quick: One of the alternatives joined by OR.
definition: The whole OR expression is a disjunction. Its joined alternatives are disjuncts. Each alternative can itself be compound, and one true disjunct is enough to make the disjunction true.
example: In (p AND q) OR r, one disjunct is p AND q and the other is r.
confusion: A disjunct can contain an AND internally; identify the outer OR first.

name: Counterassignment
quick: A truth assignment with all premises true and the proposed conclusion false.
definition: To disprove an argument’s validity, find one assignment that respects every premise but violates the conclusion. Such an assignment is a counterexample to the claimed logical consequence.
example: For p implies q, q, therefore p, choose p = F and q = T. Both premises hold, while p does not.
confusion: An assignment that makes even one premise false does not demonstrate invalidity.
